import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Betrothed numbers

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betrothed_numbers)
- [OEIS A005276](https://oeis.org/A005276)
-/

namespace BetrothedNumbers

open scoped ArithmeticFunction.sigma

/--
Two natural numbers $m$ and $n$ are **betrothed**  (or quasi-amicable) if $\sigma(m) = \sigma(n) = m + n + 1$,
where $\sigma$ is the sum-of-divisors function. Equivalently, the sum of the proper divisors
of $m$ equals $n + 1$, and the sum of the proper divisors of $n$ equals $m + 1$.
-/
@[mk_iff]
structure IsBetrothed (m n : ℕ) : Prop where
  left : σ 1 m = m + n + 1
  right : σ 1 n = m + n + 1

/-- The smallest known betrothed pair $(48, 75)$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem betrothed_48_75 : IsBetrothed 48 75 := by
  constructor <;> decide

/-- `IsBetrothed` is symmetric. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem IsBetrothed.symm {m n : ℕ} (h : IsBetrothed m n) : IsBetrothed n m := by
  rw [isBetrothed_iff] at *
  omega

/--
**Same parity betrothed numbers conjecture.**
Do there exist betrothed numbers $(m, n)$ where both have the same parity
(both even or both odd)?

All known betrothed pairs consist of one even and one odd number.

The requirement $m \neq n$ is part of the question: $\mathrm{IsBetrothed}\ n\ n$ says
$\sigma(n) = 2n + 1$, i.e. that $n$ is quasiperfect, which is the separate open problem
`QuasiperfectNumbers.exists_quasiperfect`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem same_parity_betrothed :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ m n : ℕ, m ≠ n ∧ IsBetrothed m n ∧ (Even m ↔ Even n) := by
  sorry

/--
**Infinitude of betrothed numbers conjecture.**
Are there infinitely many betrothed number pairs?

-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinitely_many_betrothed :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ × ℕ | p.1 < p.2 ∧ IsBetrothed p.1 p.2}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end BetrothedNumbers

reformulations.difference: Uses natural-number variables with positivity implicit in the sigma equations, places distinctness outside the equation-only IsBetrothed helper, and expresses equal parity as Even m ↔ Even n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The sigma equations force both numbers to be positive: sigma at zero is zero, whereas m+n+1 is positive. The identity σ₁(k) = k + sum(properDivisors k) converts the equations precisely into s(m)=n+1 and s(n)=m+1. On natural numbers, Even m ↔ Even n means either both even or both odd. The explicit m ≠ n matches the distinct two-cycles specified by Hagis–Lord and Pollack; symmetry permits ordering such a pair without changing existence. Proved the complete equivalence to this positive, distinct, proper-divisor formulation in Review.same_parity_source_equivalence.

reformulations.difference: Counts canonical ordered pairs with m < n, whereas the sources discuss betrothed pairs or individual betrothed numbers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Let S be the set used by Lean and T the set of distinct ordered pairs satisfying IsBetrothed. Symmetry gives T = S ∪ Prod.swap '' S, so S is infinite exactly when T is infinite. Each number has at most one partner, since σ₁(m)=m+n+1 uniquely determines n. Consequently, projecting T onto its first coordinate is injective and its image is exactly the set of numbers belonging to a distinct betrothed pair. Proved both equivalences in Review.infinite_ordered_equivalence and Review.infinite_numbers_equivalence.

sources_consulted: Hagis and Lord, “Quasi-Amicable Numbers”, Mathematics of Computation 31 (1977), 608–611; read through https://r.jina.ai/https://www.ams.org/journals/mcom/1977-31-138/S0025-5718-1977-0434939-3/S0025-5718-1977-0434939-3.pdf
review.notes: Checked every declaration, including the generated iff lemma and both proved tests. Both research questions remain on Wikipedia’s current unsolved-problems list. The equation-only helper permits a diagonal exactly when the number is quasiperfect, as its accompanying documentation explains; both research statements explicitly exclude that case. Lean experiments in /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiled successfully, excluded 0 and 1 in either coordinate, reproduced the first five known pairs, and verified the equivalences without sorry-dependent proofs. OEIS and the AMS paper were recovered through a text reader after direct requests returned HTTP 403. The reviewed file was confirmed byte-for-byte unchanged from the specified commit.
